steps.ask: How do you find the gradient of a straight line through two known points?
steps.title: Find the slope of l

lines.text: $l$ passes through $(6, 0)$ and $(10, 2)$.

steps.ask: If the tangent to p is parallel to l, what must be true about their slopes?
steps.title: Translate the condition into a slope

lines.text: $l'(x) = \hl{1}{\frac{1}{2}}$ for every $x$, since $l$ is a straight line.
So $p'(x) = l'(x)$ means the tangent to $p$ has slope $\hl{1}{\frac{1}{2}}$, parallel to $l$.

steps.ask: Where on the curve could a tangent have the slope of l, and how many such places are there?
steps.title: Draw the two parallel tangents

lines.text: Place a ruler along $l$ and slide it down and to the left until it just touches the curve near the lower left. Draw this tangent in blue.
Slide it up and to the right until it just touches the curve near the maximum. Draw this second tangent in blue.

steps.ask: How do you read the x-value of a touching point from the graph?
steps.title: Read the x-values from the touching points

lines.text: Draw a vertical line from each touching point down to the x-axis and read off the values.
The first touches at about $\hl{2}{x} = \hl{2}{2.2}$ and the second at about $\hl{2}{x} = \hl{2}{6.8}$.

steps.ask: What is the gradient of p(x) at each turning point, and where is it steepest?
steps.title: Read the gradient of p(x) at key points

lines.text: The value of $\hl{1}{p'(x)}$ is the gradient of $p(x)$.
At $\hl{2}{x} = \hl{2}{1}$ and $\hl{2}{x} = \hl{2}{3}$, $p(x)$ has a turning point, so the gradient is $\hl{3}{0}$: $p'(\hl{2}{1}) = \hl{3}{0}$ and $p'(\hl{2}{3}) = \hl{3}{0}$.
$p(x)$ is steepest uphill at its inflection point $\hl{2}{x} = \hl{2}{2}$, where the gradient is at its maximum, so $p'(\hl{2}{2}) = \hl{3}{1}$.
We are given $p'(\hl{2}{0}) = \hl{3}{-3}$.

steps.ask: What shape is the graph of $p'(x)$ if $p(x)$ is a cubic? Where is its line of symmetry?
steps.title: Use the shape of p'(x) to find the last point

lines.text: $p(x)$ is a cubic, so $\hl{1}{p'(x)}$ is a quadratic: a U-shape upside down, with its peak at $(\hl{2}{2}, \hl{3}{1})$.
A quadratic is symmetric about its peak, so $\hl{2}{x} = \hl{2}{4}$ matches $\hl{2}{x} = \hl{2}{0}$: $p'(\hl{2}{4}) = \hl{3}{-3}$.
